blocks.text: 1. Precision-Recall Curve
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444061168-85434402.png

Both the ROC Curve and AUC, the two previous topics, closed by flagging the exact same real weakness: on heavily imbalanced datasets, a huge count of True Negatives can dilute the False Positive Rate, making performance look deceptively strong even when a model genuinely struggles to identify the minority class. The Precision-Recall Curve was built specifically to sidestep this exact weakness, by plotting Precision against Recall, across every possible decision threshold, exactly the way the ROC Curve plots True Positive Rate against False Positive Rate.

The critical structural difference, covered in full depth throughout this topic, is that neither Precision nor Recall ever involves True Negatives in their formulas at all, both already covered in their own dedicated topics earlier in this module, which makes this curve structurally immune to the exact dilution problem that affects the ROC Curve and AUC on imbalanced data.
2. The Two Axes
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444061168-808858916.png

The Precision-Recall Curve's vertical axis is Precision, already covered in full depth in its own topic earlier in this module, True Positives divided by True Positives plus False Positives, measuring how trustworthy the model's positive predictions actually are. The horizontal axis is Recall, also already covered in its own topic, True Positives divided by True Positives plus False Negatives, measuring how thoroughly the model catches genuine positive cases.

Both of these axes are built entirely from just three of the four confusion matrix categories, True Positives, False Positives, and False Negatives. True Negatives, the fourth category first introduced back in the Accuracy topic, never appear anywhere in either axis's formula at all, a deliberate, structural design choice that turns out to matter enormously on imbalanced data, covered directly in the next section.
3. Why Excluding True Negatives Matters So Much

blocks.alt: Why Excluding True Negatives Matters So Much
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444061169-98921271.png

It is worth connecting this directly back to the exact imbalance weakness already covered in the ROC Curve and AUC topics. False Positive Rate, the ROC Curve's horizontal axis, divides by True Negatives plus False Positives. On a heavily imbalanced dataset, where True Negatives vastly outnumber every other category, even a genuinely large raw number of false positives gets diluted into a small-looking False Positive Rate, since it is being measured against such an enormous denominator.

Precision, by contrast, divides by True Positives plus False Positives, a formula that never includes True Negatives anywhere at all. This means a large number of false positives shows up directly and honestly as a meaningfully lower Precision value, with no enormous True Negative denominator available to dilute or hide it. This single structural difference, excluding True Negatives entirely from both axes, is exactly what makes the Precision-Recall Curve fundamentally more honest and trustworthy than the ROC Curve specifically on imbalanced data.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This is precisely the same underlying insight already covered for Balanced Accuracy in the Accuracy topic and for the general imbalance discussion throughout this module: metrics that avoid leaning on a large, easy majority class tend to give a far more honest picture of real classifier quality.

blocks.text: 4. How the Curve Is Built

Building a Precision-Recall Curve follows the exact same general process already covered for the ROC Curve in its own topic, just computing a different pair of quantities at each step. Starting from a classifier's predicted probabilities, exactly as required for the ROC Curve, the decision threshold is swept systematically across its entire range, from 1.0 down to 0.0.

At every threshold value along this sweep, Precision and Recall are computed for that specific threshold, rather than True Positive Rate and False Positive Rate. Each resulting pair becomes one point on the plot, and connecting every point across the full sweep traces out the complete Precision-Recall Curve, mirroring the ROC Curve's construction process exactly, with different axes.
5. Reading the Curve's Shape
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444061169-591896445.png

At a high decision threshold, the model predicts positive only when genuinely confident, resulting in very few positive predictions overall, which tends to produce high Precision, since the few positive calls made are likely correct, but low Recall, since many genuine positives get missed at such a strict, conservative bar. This corresponds to the upper-left region of the curve.

At a low decision threshold, the model predicts positive far more readily, resulting in many more positive predictions overall, which tends to produce lower Precision, since more false alarms slip through, but higher Recall, since more genuine positives get caught by this wider net. This corresponds to the lower-right region of the curve, and this entire shape traces exactly the same precision-recall tradeoff already covered conceptually in both the Precision and Recall topics, now made fully visible across the entire threshold spectrum at once.
6. A Different Kind of Baseline
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444061169-394674530.png

Recall the ROC Curve's diagonal baseline, representing pure random guessing, with True Positive Rate always exactly equal to False Positive Rate at every point along that line. The Precision-Recall Curve has a genuinely different kind of baseline: rather than a diagonal line, the random-guessing baseline here is a flat, horizontal line, sitting at a height exactly equal to the positive class's actual proportion within the overall dataset.

On a heavily imbalanced dataset, where the positive class makes up only a small fraction of the total, this baseline sits very low on the plot, close to the bottom of the chart. This has a genuinely useful practical consequence: any real improvement a model achieves above this low, honest baseline is immediately, visually obvious, in sharp contrast to the ROC Curve's fixed diagonal, which does not shift or reflect the actual class balance of the dataset being evaluated at all.
7. A Direct Comparison on Imbalanced Data

blocks.alt: A Direct Comparison on Imbalanced Data
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444061169-116464488.png

It is worth stating the core payoff of this entire topic directly, through a concrete side-by-side comparison. Evaluate the exact same weak, poorly performing model on the exact same heavily imbalanced dataset using both curves. The ROC Curve and its AUC summary, exactly as flagged in both prior topics, can look deceptively strong, since the model's many false positives get diluted and hidden by the dataset's huge True Negative count.

The Precision-Recall Curve, evaluated on that same model and that same data, honestly reveals the weakness directly, since it never references True Negatives at all in either of its two axes, meaning there is no large denominator available to hide those same false positives behind. This direct contrast is precisely why the Precision-Recall Curve is the recommended, more trustworthy choice specifically whenever working with heavily imbalanced classification problems.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Whenever working with a dataset known to be heavily imbalanced, defaulting to the Precision-Recall Curve over the ROC Curve, or at minimum reporting both side by side, is a sound, defensible practical habit worth adopting.

blocks.text: 8. Average Precision: A Single-Number Summary
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444061169-883629633.png

Exactly as AUC condenses the entire ROC Curve into one single, comparable number, Average Precision performs the same condensing role for the Precision-Recall Curve. It is computed as a weighted mean of the Precision achieved at each threshold along the curve, with the weight at each point determined by how much Recall increased at that specific step.

A higher Average Precision value indicates a stronger, more favorable Precision-Recall Curve overall, closer to the ideal upper-right corner where both Precision and Recall would simultaneously be high. Average Precision serves the exact same practical role for this curve that AUC serves for the ROC Curve, a single, directly comparable number useful for ranking or comparing several candidate models without needing to visually inspect and compare their full curves side by side.
9. Choosing Between the Two Curves

When the classes in a dataset are roughly balanced, the ROC Curve and AUC, covered in the previous two topics, work perfectly well and remain a reasonable, standard, widely understood choice, since the imbalance-driven dilution problem covered throughout this topic simply does not arise in any meaningful way on balanced data.

When classes are heavily imbalanced, and particularly when correctly identifying the minority class is the actual priority, exactly the situation already emphasized repeatedly throughout the Handling Imbalanced Data module and revisited in this module's Accuracy topic, the Precision-Recall Curve gives a genuinely more honest, more trustworthy picture of real classifier quality, and should be the preferred choice over the ROC Curve in that specific, common situation.

blocks.text: 10. The Direct Connection to F1 Score

It is worth connecting this curve directly back to F1 Score, already covered in its own topic, the harmonic mean of Precision and Recall computed at one single, fixed decision threshold. The Precision-Recall Curve shows that exact same underlying tradeoff between Precision and Recall, just across every possible threshold simultaneously rather than at just one fixed point.

Finding whichever specific threshold along this curve maximizes F1 Score corresponds to identifying one particular, specific point on the Precision-Recall Curve, the point where the harmonic mean of that threshold's Precision and Recall values is highest. This connection makes the Precision-Recall Curve a genuinely useful tool not just for visualizing the overall tradeoff, but for directly, visually identifying the specific threshold that would maximize F1 Score, or any other threshold-dependent metric of interest, for a given model.
11. Worked Example
The example below computes the Precision-Recall Curve and Average Precision for a classifier on a deliberately imbalanced dataset, directly comparing it against AUC on the same data.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve, average_precision_score, roc_auc_score
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
# A heavily imbalanced dataset: 95% negative, 5% positive
X_negative = rng.normal(loc=[0, 0], scale=2, size=(950, 2))
X_positive = rng.normal(loc=[2, 2], scale=2.5, size=(50, 2))  # meaningful overlap with negatives
X = np.vstack([X_negative, X_positive])
y = np.array([0] * 950 + [1] * 50)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42, stratify=y)

model = LogisticRegression()
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
probabilities = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

precisions, recalls, thresholds = precision_recall_curve(y_test, probabilities)
avg_precision = average_precision_score(y_test, probabilities)
auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, probabilities)

print(f"AUC: {auc:.3f}")
print(f"Average Precision: {avg_precision:.3f}")
print(f"\nPositive class proportion (the Precision-Recall baseline): {y_test.mean():.3f}")
print("Compare Average Precision against this baseline, not against 0.5 the way AUC is compared")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Notice AUC may look reasonably strong even on this imbalanced, overlapping dataset, while Average Precision, compared honestly against the low positive-class-proportion baseline rather than against 0.5, gives a more grounded sense of how much real improvement the model actually achieves.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: The Precision-Recall Curve plots Precision against Recall across every decision threshold, mirroring the ROC Curve's construction.
Neither axis ever involves True Negatives, structurally avoiding the dilution problem that affects the ROC Curve on imbalanced data.
Its random-guessing baseline is a flat line at the positive class's actual proportion, not a fixed diagonal like the ROC Curve's.
On heavily imbalanced data, this curve honestly reveals weaknesses the ROC Curve and AUC can hide behind a huge True Negative count.
Average Precision condenses the entire curve into one number, mirroring AUC's role for the ROC Curve.
ROC Curve suits roughly balanced data; the Precision-Recall Curve suits heavily imbalanced data, especially when the minority class matters most.
Maximizing F1 Score corresponds to one specific, identifiable point along this curve.
This closes out the threshold-independent, curve-based metrics in this module, following directly from Precision and Recall.
Next up: Cohen Kappa, which incorporates all four confusion matrix categories together, correcting for agreement expected by chance alone.
